newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Workers down tools at Renault car plants.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Workers down tools at Renault car plants.

text.p: Workers staged one-hour strikes at Renault factories on Friday in protest at the carmaker's plans to shut down a Belgian plant with 3,100 job losses.
After limited overnight stoppages, workers downed toools at Renault plants in Paris and elsewhere in France, with strikes scheduled throughout the day in Belgium and Spain as well.
Renault management said the strike calls had been respected by between a quarter and a third of staff at several French factories by late morning.

Despite an angry trade union riposte, Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer stuck firmly by plans to close the firm's profitable Vilvoorde factory, saying the decision, which has also provoked a storm of political protest, was traumatic but indispensable.

"It's a brutal, hard and painful decision," Schweitzer told Europe 1 radio. "It's a trauma which I understand, a trauma which I believe necessary," he said of the decision to close the Belgian plant at Vilvoorde, announced last Thursday.

Beyond the furious response from unions and staff in Europe, the closure has also been condemned by Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, whose political base is Vilvoorde, and come under fire from the European Commission in Brussels.

The fall-out spread on Friday, when the Commission announced that the Spanish government had decided to suspend a request for Brussels' approval of an 11-million-Ecu ($12.5 million) state subsidy Madrid has been planning to give for a Renault investment in Valladolid.

European Commissioner Karel Van Miert, a Belgian Socialist, had already entered the fray on Thursday, saying it was "absurd" that the firm close a profitable Belgian plant while investing with government help in Spain.

French Prime Minister Alain Juppe has asked Schweitzer to meet Belgian staff representatives as soon as possible and a meeting of the company's European works council of employers and worker representatives has been set for next Tuesday in Paris, a day unions are planning a further demonstration.
"I hope these 3,100 people will find another job...that they will continue to make their living, with others or with other Renault factories in France," Schweitzer said.
Schweitzer said the decision was taken to secure Renault's future and he now hoped for a dialogue with unions. "They're not yet at the stage where they accept a dialogue," he said.
"The reality is harsh, but it's the reality," he said. "If we do nothing the company will die."
"European growth, car sector growth is slow," he said adding that securing Renault's growth depended on tapping into "markets other than European ones".

"There will be other cuts in staff in France but there will not be other restructuring plans between now and the year 2000 because we have, in the wake of the Vilvoorde decision, an industrial balance," he added.
Renault has already said 2,700 job losses in France are also in the pipeline as it restructures amid cut-throat competition and price-cutting in a depressed market.

Asked if the French government, still a shareholder to the tune of 46 percent in Renault, had any intention of moving to push him out of his post, Schweitzer replied, "Not that I know" and added that he himself was not planning any such move.
Renault's shares had soared in the wake of the announcement last Thursday, but have suffered since as investors worry about whether the political risk could stop it coming to fruition.

Renault shares opened lower in Paris and were trading 1.65 percent down at 137.5 francs at 1140 GMT after dipping even lower shortly after the stock exchange opened. ($ = 0.881 European Currency Unit ECUs)
